note.headline: Meta slips 2.38% to 626.41; cash flow still too thin for the price

summary.thesis: Meta's sales are still growing fast at 27.53%, but free cash flow fell from 44.8B to 28.6B, and the price only makes sense if that cash flow recovers.
summary.decision: Long-term: wait. Swing: wait. The decisive test is the 2027-01-27 report, and the price is not yet at a level that pays for the risk.
summary.act_at: Long-term buy zone near 475.85; swing only on a hold of 605.33–611.95

note.happening: Meta fell 2.38% to 626.41. That puts it just below its 200-day average of 629.58 and well below its 50-day average of 679.91, and the trend is down. TechCrunch reported that Instagram now lets creators add Amazon affiliate links to reels and feed posts. The next earnings report is due on 2027-01-27.
note.business: The business itself is still expanding. Trailing revenue reached 241.6B, up from 189.5B, and growth was 27.53% over the trailing year. The gross margin, which is what is left from each sale after direct costs, is still high at 81.03%. The weak spot is profit and cash. The operating margin fell from 43.23% to 32.86%. Free cash flow, the cash left after running and investing in the business, fell from 44.8B to 28.6B. Quarterly growth also slowed, from 33.08% two quarters ago to 26.07%. The filings flag that profit per share is lagging sales and that the company missed forecasts last quarter by 29%. Heavy spending on AI is the likely cause of the drop in cash flow (general knowledge), but DATA does not split out capital spending. The balance sheet has moved to slight net debt: net cash is -1.2B, with 83.7B of debt against 11.2B of cash, though available liquidity is 82.4B. The Instagram affiliate-link feature could become a small new commerce income stream (general knowledge), but it does not change the margin or cash picture today. The insider sales of $14.2M made outside pre-set plans are a governance note, not a business change. At risk: margins and cash conversion. Not at risk: demand for the core product.

worth.text: The methods disagree sharply, and one assumption drives the gap: whether cash flow recovers. Measured on earnings and sales, the stock does not look expensive. It trades at 21.4 times trailing earnings and 6.7 times sales. That is close to the peer median of 6.4, the growth-adjusted ratio against peers is 1.01, and the price-to-sales ratio sits at only the 42nd percentile of its own 5-year history. On that basis, Meta's own sales history puts value between 475.85 and 881.21, with a middle of 707.21. A discounted cash flow model (DCF), which values today's free cash flow of 28.6B at a 10.1% discount rate, gives much less: 245.54 in the bear case, 375.79 in the base case and 511.67 in the bull case. To justify the current price, free cash flow would need to start growing at about 38.3% a year. Even 30% starting growth gives only 463.29. If the operating margin fell to 24%, value would drop to 237.86. My range runs from 475.85, where the case no longer depends on a full margin recovery, to 707.21, where the price would assume the recovery has already happened. The current price of 626.41 sits in the upper half of that range.
worth.key_assumption: Free cash flow recovers toward the earlier 44.8B as the spending pays off, instead of staying near 28.6B.
